subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 46-year-old man reports burning retrosternal discomfort after meals and at night, regurgitation of acidic material, and a chronic cough with hoarseness. He has mild asthma. His symptoms improve with antacids.
question: Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of his most likely condition?

options.text: Degeneration of NO/VIP inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus
A coordinated increase in LES resting pressure
Fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle with reduced LES pressure
Transient decreases in lower esophageal sphincter tone
Dilatation of submucosal veins in the distal esophagus

explanation_correct: GERD results from transient decreases in lower esophageal sphincter tone, allowing gastric contents to reflux into the esophagus. Typical manifestations are heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia, and it can present atypically with chronic cough, hoarseness from laryngopharyngeal reflux, and an association with asthma. Complications of long-standing disease include erosive esophagitis, strictures, and Barrett esophagus. The response to antacids supports an acid-mediated process.

explanation_incorrect.A: Loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus causes achalasia, a hypertonic nonrelaxing LES with dysphagia, not reflux.
explanation_incorrect.B: Increased LES resting pressure is the manometric hallmark of achalasia and would actually protect against reflux.
explanation_incorrect.C: Esophageal smooth muscle fibrosis with low LES pressure occurs in scleroderma (CREST) and can cause reflux, but it is not the mechanism of uncomplicated GERD.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dilated distal submucosal veins are esophageal varices from portal hypertension, which present with hematemesis rather than heartburn.

educationalObjective: GERD results from transient decreases in LES tone, producing heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia, plus extraesophageal symptoms such as chronic cough and hoarseness.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 68-year-old woman develops painful swallowing several weeks after starting an oral medication for osteoporosis. She takes the tablet with only a small sip of water and often lies down shortly afterward. Endoscopy shows a localized area of mucosal injury in the mid esophagus.
question: Which of the following medications is most likely responsible for this patient's esophagitis?
explanation_correct: Medication-induced (pill-induced) esophagitis is caused by direct mucosal injury from drugs such as bisphosphonates, tetracyclines, NSAIDs, ferrous sulfate, and potassium chloride. Bisphosphonates used for osteoporosis are a classic culprit, especially when the pill is swallowed with insufficient water or before lying down, allowing prolonged contact with the esophageal mucosa. The temporal relationship to starting the drug and the focal mid-esophageal injury support this diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Insulin is given subcutaneously and does not contact the esophageal mucosa; it is not a cause of medication-induced esophagitis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Inhaled corticosteroids primarily affect the oropharynx (eg, thrush) and are not among the classic pill-induced esophagitis agents.
explanation_incorrect.D: Proton pump inhibitors reduce acid and are used to treat reflux esophagitis, not to cause direct mucosal injury.
explanation_incorrect.E: Antifungal lozenges treat Candida esophagitis; they are not among the classic causes of medication-induced esophagitis.

educationalObjective: Medication-induced esophagitis is caused by bisphosphonates, tetracyclines, NSAIDs, ferrous sulfate, and potassium chloride, especially when pills are swallowed with little water.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 35-year-old man with advanced HIV infection and a CD4 count of 60/mm3 has 3 weeks of odynophagia and difficulty swallowing. Endoscopy reveals white, adherent pseudomembranes lining the esophageal mucosa.
question: Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation_correct: Candida is the most common infectious esophagitis, particularly in immunosuppressed patients such as those with advanced HIV. It characteristically produces white pseudomembranes or plaques on the esophageal mucosa and causes odynophagia and dysphagia. The other infectious esophagitides have distinct appearances: HSV-1 causes punched-out ulcers and CMV causes linear ulcers. Reflux and eosinophilic esophagitis are not infectious and do not form pseudomembranes.

explanation_incorrect.B: HSV-1 esophagitis produces discrete punched-out ulcers rather than confluent white pseudomembranes.
explanation_incorrect.C: CMV esophagitis causes linear ulcers in immunosuppressed patients, not white plaques.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reflux (erosive) esophagitis is the most common esophagitis overall but causes linear erosions from acid, not pseudomembranes, and is not defined by immunosuppression.
explanation_incorrect.E: Eosinophilic esophagitis is an atopic, eosinophil-predominant disease with rings and linear furrows, not infectious pseudomembranes.

educationalObjective: Candida is the most common infectious esophagitis in immunosuppressed patients and appears as white pseudomembranes; HSV-1 causes punched-out ulcers and CMV causes linear ulcers.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 22-year-old man with a long history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, and seasonal allergies presents with slowly progressive dysphagia and episodes of food impaction. Endoscopy shows concentric esophageal rings and linear furrows, and biopsy reveals numerous eosinophils in the mucosa. LES pressure on manometry is normal.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's dysphagia?
explanation_correct: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic, immune-mediated, eosinophil-predominant inflammatory disease strongly associated with atopic disorders such as asthma, eczema, and allergies. Endoscopy classically shows concentric esophageal rings and linear furrows, and biopsy confirms eosinophilic infiltration. It causes dysphagia and food impaction, particularly in young atopic patients, and the normal LES pressure helps exclude a primary motility disorder such as achalasia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Reflux esophagitis is due to acid injury from GERD and shows erosions, not eosinophil-predominant inflammation with rings and furrows in an atopic patient.
explanation_incorrect.B: Candida infection produces white pseudomembranes in immunosuppressed patients, not concentric rings with an eosinophilic infiltrate.
explanation_incorrect.C: HSV-1 causes punched-out ulcers, typically in immunocompromised hosts, and does not produce rings or linear furrows.
explanation_incorrect.D: Medication-induced esophagitis follows ingestion of offending pills (eg, bisphosphonates, tetracyclines, potassium chloride) and causes focal injury, not a chronic atopic eosinophilic pattern.

educationalObjective: Eosinophilic esophagitis is a chronic immune-mediated, eosinophil-predominant disease associated with atopy, with rings and linear furrows on endoscopy.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 58-year-old man has had long-standing heartburn and regurgitation for more than a decade. He is concerned about the complications of his condition and asks what might develop if it continues untreated.
question: Which of the following is a recognized complication of chronic GERD?
explanation_correct: Chronic GERD exposes the distal esophageal mucosa to repeated acid injury, leading to complications that include erosive (reflux) esophagitis, peptic strictures, and Barrett esophagus. Barrett esophagus is specialized intestinal metaplasia that replaces the normal squamous lining and predisposes to esophageal adenocarcinoma. It is therefore a key complication to recognize and surveillance is often recommended.

explanation_incorrect.A: Achalasia is a primary motility disorder from loss of myenteric inhibitory neurons, not a complication of reflux.
explanation_incorrect.C: Plummer-Vinson syndrome is the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anemia, and esophageal webs with increased squamous cell carcinoma risk; it is not caused by GERD.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a partial-thickness mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction from forceful vomiting, not a reflux complication.
explanation_incorrect.E: Esophageal varices result from portal hypertension, usually due to cirrhosis, not from gastroesophageal reflux.

educationalObjective: Chronic GERD can cause erosive esophagitis, strictures, and Barrett esophagus (intestinal metaplasia), which predisposes to esophageal adenocarcinoma.
